newsitem.title: USA: Mass. legislators pass $18.3 bln FY 1998 budget.
newsitem.headline: Mass. legislators pass $18.3 bln FY 1998 budget.

text.p: The Massachusetts Legislature passed an $18.3 billion spending plan late on Monday that gives the taxpayers a modest cut, boosts spending for higher education and the courts and moves towards eliminating Middlesex County.

The revenues from Fiscal 1997, which gave way to Fiscal Year 1998 at midnight, will not be fully tabulated and certified until this fall. When the exact total of fiscal 1997 revenues are known, budget committee leaders promised, issues not completely encompassed in the $18.3 billion budget will be addressed.
Among those issues are easing pressure on the state's capital budget and increasing the scope of some tax cuts, State House News Service reported.

The spending blueprint does endorse three tax-cutting proposals. It creates an earned income tax credit that "piggybacks" on the existing federal credit that is available to low-income working families.

The state's credit would be worth 10 percent of the federal one. It also allows homeowners faced with costly septic tank repairs and upgrades to write off up to $6,000 on their taxes Additionally, the budget doubles the dependent child care deduction to $1,200 per child 12 and under.

The uncertainty of FY '97's final figures caused the conferees to pay only $23 million of the $134 million due for the final payment of the bonds issued in 1990 to bail the state out of its fiscal crisis. The Senate version of the budget paid off the entire amount, but the compromise package, Haley said, will use FY '98 funds to pay off the remaining $111 million.
Gov. William Weld is expected to take the full 10 days before signing the document, meaning that a fiscal year will begin without a new budget for the first time in three years.
Although the Senate's budget eliminated all 14 counties in the state, the House hedged, and no county language was included in the document.

However, Senate Ways and Means Committee members unanimously approved a separate bill that abolishes the financially troubled Middlesex County effective tomorrow, and Hampden, and Worcester counties on July 1, 1998.
The conference committee put out a statement saying that language represented the compromise position of the House and Senate negotiators.
* increasing funding for public higher education campuses to $743.3 million, an 8 percent hike
* increasing community policing grants by $5 million * increasing state recycling effforts by 42 percent, totalling $7 million

* continuing the phaseout of a diversion into state coffers of Lottery revenues that are supposed to go to cities and towns. The budget provides an additional $55.5 million in Lottery revenues to communities.
* fully funding the latest installment of education reform money, an increase of $222 million
* allocating $470 million for the courts, an increase of $37.6 million.

Michael Widmer of the Massachusetts Taxpayers Federation praised the budget, but did say he is "mildly concerned" about the state's ability to maintain in the future the commitments conferees made in several accounts, particularly higher education.
